title: Trainees explore Community Engagement
content:
How can heritage practitioners create meaningful opportunities for communities to shape the ways their heritage is understood, cared for and shared? This question guided HERITΛGE’s recent four-day online workshop, Engaging Communities in Cultural Heritage, which brought together 23 participants from 18 countries.

Participants joined from Poland, Lebanon, Italy, Iraq, Albania, Greece, Armenia, Rwanda, Serbia, Latvia, Mauritius, India, Egypt, Iran, South Africa, Kenya, Palestine and Nepal to explore 

The programme examined different understandings of community, identity, belonging and relationships with heritage, while emphasising the importance of positionality, research, inclusion, accessibility and meaningful participation. 

Participants were introduced to approaches including Asset-Based Community Development, asset mapping and ethnographic research, exploring how community assets, knowledge, relationships and networks can inform the design and implementation of engagement activities.

title: Oral History and Heritage workshop in Monterrey
content:
On October 8 and 9, HERITΛGE held the in-person Oral History and Heritage workshop at the Museo Estatal de Culturas Populares de Nuevo León. The workshop – part of our HerMaP Mexico initiative – provided a space for learning and exchange focused on the use of oral history to document, preserve, and transmit cultural heritage and community memory. The program combined methodological tools, ethical considerations, and practical exercises applied to heritage projects.

The workshop brought together a group of eight participants working with Indigenous communities and cultural heritage projects, bringing diverse experiences and perspectives and representing at least five Indigenous peoples residing in Nuevo León. This exchange provided an opportunity to reflect on oral history not only as a documentation methodology, but also as a tool for strengthening the transmission of memories, knowledge, and living cultural practices.

title: Celebrating European Heritage Days at the RCH launch in Marseille
content:
Alexandre Causse from RCH Co-ordinator FSP declaring the opening of the Kick off event

The Heritage Management Organization (HERITΛGE) marked this year’s European Heritage Days by joining our fellow consortium partners and hundreds of cultural heritage and climate professionals, researchers, policymakers and other stakeholders from around the world for the launch of the European Partnership for Resilient Cultural Heritage (RCH) in Marseille, France. RCH is co-funded by the European Union. 

With the 2026 European Heritage Days theme, “Heritage at Risk: Revive, Resist, Reimagine,” the gathering offered a timely opportunity to turn attention towards the future of heritage in a changing climate—and the role heritage itself can play in helping communities adapt.

title: A visit to Red Rock Centre in Rwanda
content:
Mark chatting to community members in the Red Rocks centre.

By Mark Goldstone* 

Ochre burnt-orange dust, which for convenience we call red, covers both the outside and the inside of my 4×4. Everything is a hill in Rwanda, and my trip today takes me up a thousand hills and down a thousand more. Power takes me up and gravity takes me down like a marble in a marble run. 

My destination is the Red Rocks Intercultural Exchange Centre in Rwanda’s highlands outside the city of Musanze. The journey is hard and I arrive tired and dusty, but within five minutes every member of staff knows my name. This is the kind of welcome you can expect at Red Rocks, a community-based initiative  working with communities living alongside protected areas and important natural ecosystems that has received one of HERITΛGE’s small grants for African projects and is also the recipient of another grant, fiscally sponsored by HERITΛGE.

title: 10 proyectos de patrimonio del norte de México reciben apoyos
content:
The Heritage Management Organization (HERITΛGE) se complace en anunciar los 10 proyectos seleccionados para recibir apoyo a través de HerMaP México, su principal iniciativa para fortalecer la gestión del patrimonio cultural en la región fronteriza del norte de México.

Los proyectos seleccionados representan a Baja California, Sonora, Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León y Tamaulipas, garantizando así la representación de los seis estados que conforman el ámbito geográfico de HerMaP México en esta primera convocatoria de apoyos.

Los proyectos fueron seleccionados entre 115 solicitudes recibidas a través de una convocatoria abierta lanzada a principios de 2026, reflejando tanto la extraordinaria riqueza del patrimonio cultural de la región como el compromiso de las comunidades, profesionales e instituciones que trabajan para salvaguardarlo.

title: Ten Heritage Projects in N. Mexico Receive Funding
content:
The Heritage Management Organization (HERITΛGE) is delighted to announce the 10 projects selected to receive funding through HerMaP Mexico, its major initiative to strengthen cultural heritage management across Mexico’s northern border region.

The selected projects represent Baja California, Sonora, Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas, ensuring that all six states within HerMaP Mexico’s geographic scope are represented in this first round of funding.

The projects were chosen from 115 applications submitted through an open call launched in early 2026, demonstrating both the extraordinary richness of the region’s cultural heritage and the commitment of communities, practitioners and institutions working to safeguard it. 

The selected initiatives offer a window onto the remarkable diversity of northern Mexico. They encompass heritage ranging from traditional farming techniques and gastronomic traditions to crafts, music, memorial sites, museums and the photographic documentation of intangible cultural heritage. They are rooted in landscapes that stretch from ocean coasts and vast deserts to mountain regions and complex urban environments.

title: Ghanaian Heritage Scholar Named First Graduate of HERITΛGE Memorial Scholarship
content:
Dr. Emmanuel Banahene Owusu, lecturer in the Department of Architecture at Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Kumasi, Ghana, has become the first scholar to graduate under the Angela Bugeja, Molly Hude and Ioanna Thomopoulou Memorial Scholarship. He completed the Certificate in Digital Tools for Heritage Management, a 30 ECTS academic certificate delivered jointly by HERITΛGE (The Heritage Management Organization) and HOGENT.

The award commemorates Angela Bugeja of Malta, Molly Hude of the United States, and Ioanna Thomopoulou of Greece, students of the HERITΛGE MA in Heritage Management who passed prematurely on July 3, 2013, at the end of their fieldwork in Belize.

They gave a great deal to HERITΛGE in its early years, and the annual scholarship exists so that their names, and their contribution, are carried forward by other heritage professionals.

title: Community Lab: 17 Heritage Professionals Complete the EMPATHS Training Programme
content:
The programme’s second, in-person phase—the Community Lab: Developing Heritage Interpretation Skills through Participatory Approaches—took place from 28 August to 1 September 2026 at the Ethnological Museum of Thrace in Alexandroupoli, Greece. Participants had the opportunity to put into practice the knowledge and tools acquired during the programme’s initial online phase by working with local communities and co-creating approaches to cultural heritage interpretation.

At a time when the way we interpret heritage plays a crucial role in shaping the communities we build, the need for more participatory, inclusive, and collaborative approaches is more relevant than ever. The EMPATHS training programme seeks to develop an accessible framework and participatory methodology, equipping heritage professionals with the tools they need to engage actively with communities and co-create narratives that reflect diverse voices and experiences.

title: Roundtable: Heritage as a Driver of Community and Economic Development
content:
To celebrate the start of a new academic year, HERITΛGE is proud to host a public roundtable bringing together distinguished heritage leaders from five African countries. The discussion will explore how heritage—and its effective management—can serve as a lever for community and economic development, and how this potential is being approached in different national contexts.

The roundtable marks the opening of a special edition of HERITΛGE’s Community and Economic Development workshop for heritage professionals in Africa. Around 30 participants from Ethiopia, The Gambia, Ghana, Kenya and Rwanda will take part in the programme, developing the knowledge and practical tools needed to create sustainable economic and social benefits through heritage.

Joining the roundtable:

Essel Blankson – Executive Director, Ghana Museums & Monuments Board

Dr Fredrick Manthi – Director of Antiquities, Sites and Monuments, National Museums of Kenya

Abebaw Ayalew Gella – Director General, Ethiopian Heritage Authority

Amb. Robert Masozera – Director General, Rwanda Cultural Heritage Academy

Sanna B. Jarju – Director of Literature, Performing and Fine Arts, National Centre for Arts and Culture, The Gambia

title: Museum As a Space for Healing? Towards Reparative Discomfort.
content:
The Gate of No Return in Ouidah, Benin, commemorating the millions of enslaved Africans

By Philip Kwame Boafo, PhD

The museum has long been imagined as a place of preservation, education, and in recent times healing. Yet I wonder whether healing has become one of the most convenient metaphors through which museums avoid the harder work of confronting history. I have been contemplating on this question a lot lately, which is, if the museum heals too quickly, what kinds of wounds does it leave untouched?
